'''''Tilia americana''''' is a species of [[tree]] in the family [[Malvaceae]]. It is native to eastern [[North America]], from southeast [[Manitoba]] east to [[New Brunswick]], southwest to northeast [[Oklahoma]], southeast to [[South Carolina]], and west along the [[Niobrara River]] to [[Cherry County, Nebraska]]. It is the sole representative of its genus in the Western Hemisphere, assuming ''[[Tilia caroliniana|T. caroliniana]]'' is treated as a subspecies or local ecotype of ''T. americana''.<ref name=usfs>{{Silvics |volume=2 |genus=Tilia |species=americana |first=T. R. |last=Crow}}</ref><ref name=grin>{{GRIN|id=36668|name=Tilia americana}}</ref> Common names include '''American basswood'''<ref>{{PLANTS|id=TIAM|taxon=Tilia americana|access-date=10 December 2015}}</ref> and '''American linden'''.

== Description ==
[[File:Tilia americana, Arnold Arboretum - IMG 5911.JPG|left|thumb|A specimen in the [[Arnold Arboretum]] leafing out in spring]]

The American basswood is a medium-sized to large [[deciduous]] tree reaching a height of {{convert|18 to 37|m|ft|round=5|abbr=on}} exceptionally {{convert|39|m|ft|abbr=on}} with a trunk diameter of {{convert|1-1.5|m|ft|0|abbr=on}} at maturity. It grows faster than many North American hardwoods, often twice the annual growth rate of [[American beech]] and many [[birch]] species. Life expectancy is around 200 years, with flowering and seeding generally occurring between 15 and 100 years, though occasionally seed production may start as early as eight years.

The crown is domed, the branches spreading, often pendulous. The [[Bark (botany)|bark]] is gray to light brown, with narrow, well defined fissures. The [[root]]s are large, deep, and spreading. The [[twig]]s are smooth, reddish-green, becoming light gray in their second year, finally dark brown or brownish gray, marked with dark wart-like excrescences. The winter buds are stout, ovate-acute, smooth, deep red, with two bud scales visible.

The [[leaves]] are [[simple leaf|simple]], [[alternate leaf|alternately]] arranged, [[Glossary of leaf morphology#ovate|ovate]] to [[Cordate (leaf shape)|cordate]], asymmetrical, unequal at the base (the side nearer the branch the larger), {{convert|10–15|cm|0|abbr=on}} (can grow up to {{convert|25|cm|0|disp=or|abbr=on}}) long and broad, with a long, slender petiole, a coarsely serrated margin and an acuminate apex. [[William Jackson Bean]] noted that occasionally, enormous leaves measuring {{convert|38|cm|0|disp=or|abbr=on}} long by {{convert|25|cm|0|disp=or|abbr=on}} wide appear on thick, succulent shoots.<ref name=Bean/> They open from the bud conduplicate, pale green, downy; when full grown are dark green, smooth, shining above, paler beneath, with tufts of rusty brown hairs in the axils of the primary veins; the small [[stipule]]s fall soon after leaf opening. The fall color is yellow-green to yellow. Both the twigs and leaves contain [[mucilaginous]] sap.

The [[flower]]s are small, fragrant, yellowish-white, {{convert|10–14|mm|frac=32|abbr=in}} in diameter, arranged in drooping, [[cymose]] clusters of 6–20 with a whitish-green leaf-like [[bract]] attached for half its length at the base of the cyme. They are perfect, regular, with five [[sepal]]s and [[petal]]s, numerous [[stamen]]s, and a five-celled superior [[ovary (botany)|ovary]]. The leaves emerge in mid-spring, but the flowers require day lengths of approximately 14 hours and 30 minutes to form, hence ''T. americana''{{'}}s range is limited to north of the [[35th parallel north|35th parallel]]. Time of flowering varies by several weeks depending on the latitude; early May in Canada and early June in the extreme southern extent. Leaf drop in fall occurs between early and late October depending on the latitude. The flowers are fragrant and insect-pollinated.

The [[fruit]] is a small, [[globose]], downy, hard and dry cream-colored [[nutlet]] with a diameter of {{convert|8–10|mm|frac=32|abbr=on}}.<ref name=usfs /><ref name=nrcs>USDA NRCS Tree Guide: [https://plants.usda.gov/plantguide/pdf/cs_tiama.pdf ''Tilia americana'' (pdf file)]</ref><ref name=Keeler>{{cite book | last =Keeler | first =H. L. | title =Our Native Trees and How to Identify Them | url =https://archive.org/details/ournativetreesa02keelgoog | publisher =Charles Scribner's Sons | year =1900 | location =New York | pages =[https://archive.org/details/ournativetreesa02keelgoog/page/n51 24]–31 }}</ref>

== Ecology ==
American basswood is dominant in the sugar maple–basswood forest association, which is most common in western [[Wisconsin]] and central [[Minnesota]], but occurs as far east as [[New England]] and southern [[Quebec]] in places that have [[mesic habitat|mesic]] soil with relatively high [[soil pH|pH]]. It also has minor occurrence in many other forest cover types.

Its flowers provide abundant nectar for insects. The seeds are eaten by [[chipmunk]]s, [[mice]], and [[squirrel]]s. [[Rabbit]]s and [[vole]]s eat the bark, sometimes girdling young trees. The leaves serve as food for [[caterpillar]]s of various [[Lepidoptera]] (see Lepidoptera which feed on ''Tilia''). The [[Bucculatricidae|ribbed cocoon maker]] species ''[[Bucculatrix improvisa]]'' has not been found on other plants.

This species is particularly susceptible to adult [[Japanese beetle]]s (an [[invasive species]] in North America) that feed on its leaves.<ref>{{cite web |publisher=USDA |title=Managing the Japanese Beetle:A Homeowner's Handbook |url=http://www.aphis.usda.gov/publications/plant_health/content/printable_version/JB3-07.indd.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140916070734/http://www.aphis.usda.gov/publications/plant_health/content/printable_version/JB3-07.indd.pdf |archive-date=2014-09-16 }}</ref> The mushroom ''[[Pholiota squarrosoides]]'' is known to decay the logs of the tree.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Halama |first=Marek |date=January 2011 |title=First record of the rare species Pholiota squarrosoides (Agaricales, Strophariaceae) in southwestern Poland |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/236153077
|journal=Polish Botanical Journal |access-date=August 10, 2019}}</ref>

== Cultivation and uses ==
[[File:Tilia americana sections.jpg|thumb|upright=1.2|Sections of ''Tilia americana'' from ''[[The American Woods]]'']]

''T. americana'' mostly spreads by self-[[coppicing]] rather than seeds. Juvenile basswoods coppice readily, and even old trees may sprout from the stump if cut. ''T. americana'' seeds have a low viability rate of approximately 30%, and seeds develop an unusually hard seed coating after reaching maturity. This seed coating can delay germination for up to two years. It is possible to gather seeds in early autumn to sow before they dry out and form the harder coating.

The American basswood is recommended as an ornamental tree when the mass of foliage or a deep shade is desired; no native tree surpasses it in this respect. It is often planted on the windward side of an orchard as a protection to young and delicate trees.<ref name=Keeler /> It is cultivated at least as far north as [[Juneau, Alaska]].<ref>Juneau: [http://www.silverbowinn.com/downtown_tree_guide%20final%2006.pdf Downtown Juneau Tree Guide] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070818004459/http://www.silverbowinn.com/downtown_tree_guide%20final%2006.pdf |date=August 18, 2007 }}</ref>

The foliage and flowers are both edible, though the tender young leaves are more palatable. It is a beneficial species for attracting pollinators as well. Bees produce excellent honey with a mildly spicy flavor from its blossoms. The inner bark was used historically as a fiber source for making baskets, rope, and fishing nets.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Sullivan |first1=Janet |title=SPECIES: Tilia americana |url=https://www.fs.fed.us/database/feis/plants/tree/tilame/all.html |website=Fire Effects Information System (FEIS) FEIS Home Page Index of Species Information |publisher=USDA |access-date=17 August 2019}}</ref>

Basswood attracts many insect pests, including [[Japanese beetle]]s, and skeletonized leaves are common. Mite galls commonly form on the foliage.

[[Cultivar]]s include 'Nova', 'Duros' (with an upright crown), the pyramidal 'Frontyard' and the conic-crowned 'Redmond'.

The tree was introduced to the UK in 1752, but has never prospered there, being prone to dieback.<ref name=Bean>{{cite book |last=Bean |first=W. J. |year=1921 |title=Trees and shrubs hardy in the British Isles |edition=3rd |volume=II |page=590 |location=London |publisher=John Murray |oclc=5916772 }}</ref>

=== Wood ===
The wood is pale brown, sometimes nearly white or faintly tinged with red; light, soft with fine close grain; clear of knots but does not split easily. It is low in strength and has a poor steam-bending classification. It can take stains and polish without difficulty and it planes, glues, screws and nails well.<ref>{{cite book |last=Porter |first=Terry |date=2006 |title=Wood Identification & Use |edition=Revised & Expanded |page=254 |isbn=1-86108-436-6 }}</ref> It is sold generally under the name basswood. It has a [[density]] of 0.4525 (relative to water). The wood is considered odorless. This makes it valuable in the manufacture of wooden utensils and furniture. It is also used for woodcarving. The inner bark is very tough and fibrous, used in the past for making ropes.<ref name=Keeler />

Basswood is a [[tonewood]] commonly used in the manufacture of solid-body [[electric guitar]]s. It is relatively lightweight and easy to work and sand.<ref>{{cite web |title=What is Basswood? {{!}} Everything You Need to Know About Basswood |url=https://www.timberblogger.com/what-is-basswood/ |website=Timber Blogger |access-date=16 December 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221215234443/https://www.timberblogger.com/what-is-basswood/ |archive-date=15 December 2022 |date=29 June 2021}}</ref> It accepts paint and [[Wood finishing|finishes]] very well. It is usually used for guitars that will be painted an opaque color as its lack of notable grain makes it an unattractive candidate for transparent finish. It exhibits a very balanced,<ref name="guitar_tone_woods">{{cite web |title=Guitar Tone Woods |url=https://www.soundunlimited.co.uk/blogs/articles/guitar_tone_woods |website=SoundUnlimited |access-date=16 December 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221216193716/https://www.soundunlimited.co.uk/blogs/articles/guitar_tone_woods |archive-date=16 December 2022 |language=en}}</ref> even tone with a good low/mid-midrange projection making it suitable for a wide variety of musical applications.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Nusselder |first1=Joost |title=Best wood for electric guitars {{!}} Full guide matching wood & tone |url=https://neaera.com/best-wood-for-electric-guitars/#Best_mids_Basswood |website=Neaera |access-date=16 December 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221215234443/https://neaera.com/best-wood-for-electric-guitars/#Best_mids_Basswood |archive-date=15 December 2022 |language=en-us |date=16 September 2022}}</ref> It is often paired with maple laminates to balance the midrange with more treble (inherent to maple) to make a very well rounded sounding instrument. It is also relatively inexpensive, which has made it a favorite of large factories mass-producing instruments.

It has proven especially popular in instruments made for musicians who play [[heavy metal music|heavy metal]]. This could be because its tonality helps level out the thin, tinny sound associated with [[Floyd Rose|knife edged tremolo]] contacts that many modern rock and metal players use as bridges on their guitars.<ref name="guitar_tone_woods" />

Recently, basswood was used in the development of "Nxylon", a super-black material discovered by [[University of British Columbia]] researchers.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-07-30 |title=UBC super-black wood can improve telescopes, optical devices and consumer goods |url=https://news.ubc.ca/2024/07/ubc-super-black-wood-nxylon/ |access-date=2024-08-07 |website=UBC News |language=en-US}}</ref> As the primary wood used to create Nxylon, basswood's natural properties contribute to the material's lightweight, stiff structure that can be easily cut into intricate shapes. The use of basswood in Nxylon demonstrates how a common, sustainable resource can be transformed into a high-tech material with applications in fine jewelry, solar cells, and precision optical devices.

=== Medicinal uses ===
Although ''[[Tilia cordata]]'' is believed to be stronger, ''T. americana'' is also used medicinally. The dried flowers are mildly sweet and sticky, and the fruit is somewhat sweet and [[mucilaginous]]. Linden tea has a pleasing taste, due to the aromatic volatile oil found in the flowers. The flowers, leaves, wood, and charcoal (obtained from the wood) are used for medicinal purposes. Active ingredients in the linden flowers include [[flavonoid]]s (which act as [[antioxidant]]s), volatile oils, and mucilaginous constituents (which soothe and reduce inflammation).{{medcn|date=June 2025}} The plant also contains [[tannin]]s that can act as an [[astringent]].<ref name=bradley>{{citation |editor-first=Bradley |editor-last=P |title=British Herbal Compendium |volume=I |place=Dorset (Great Britain |publisher=British Herbal Medicine Association |date=1992 |pages=142–144}}</ref>

Linden flowers are used in colds, cough, fever, infections, inflammation, high blood pressure, headache (particularly migraine), as a diuretic (increases urine production), antispasmodic (reduces smooth muscle spasm along the digestive tract), and sedative.{{medcn|date=June 2025}} The flowers were added to baths to quell hysteria, and steeped as a tea to relieve anxiety-related indigestion, irregular heartbeat, and vomiting. The leaves are used to promote sweating to reduce fevers. The wood is used for liver and gallbladder disorders and cellulitis (inflammation of the skin and surrounding soft tissue). The wood burned to charcoal is ingested to treat intestinal disorders and used topically to treat edema or infection, such as cellulitis or ulcers of the lower leg.<ref name=bradley /><ref name="mice"/>
